newsitem.title: USA: US bonds regain composure, Greenspan effect brief.
newsitem.headline: US bonds regain composure, Greenspan effect brief.

text.p: Calm prevailed in the U.S. Treasury market on Monday, as players took the weekend to digest Alan Greenspan's latest remarks, which caused a sharp sell-off in financial markets worldwide on Friday.
Markets across the globe rebounded Monday, as financial officials around the world called Friday's selloffs an overreaction.
"We feel to some extent there was an overreaction to a question and the markets seem stable again," Hans Tietmeyer, Bundesbank chief and chairman of the G-10 central bankers, said.

The Federal Reserve chief spooked markets when he wondered aloud on Thursday night in a speech whether U.S. asset prices were too high. Greenspan also noted that while current inflation levels are fine, their future course is unclear.

Along with a worldwide plunge in stocks, U.S. Treasuries were hit hard Friday, with the long bond falling as much as 1-1/2 points and ending the day just 2/32 below Thursday's levels. Treasuries continued to rally Monday, with the March bond contract ending 18/32 higher, and the 30-year cash bond rising over half a point.
U.S. Stocks also rebounded on Monday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 82 points, wiping out Friday's 55 point retreat.
Market participants said the initial knee-jerk reaction to Greenspan's comments was based on fear the Fed might hike interest rates to deflate the surge in stock prices.

"Once people sat down to think about it, they realized the Fed is not going to raise rates to prick a stock market bubble if there is not a legitimate fundamental reason to raise rates," said Steve Wood, director of financial markets research at BA Securities Inc.
"With increasing evidence of moderating economic performance with limited inflation, there is not much likelihood the Fed will raise rates," he said.
But Wood added that should growth slow even more, the boom in the stock market could make it tougher for the Fed to ease.

"But I expect that in a week from now, people won't even remember Greenspan gave a speech and especially after next Tuesday when the Fed doesn't do anything (at its policy setting meeting) the market will look at how the Christmas shopping is shaping up and how it relates to growth and monetary policy down the road," Wood said.

Bond market participants had slowly been pricing in an ease as the Fed's next move, given a two-year note yield that had fallen to 5.59 percent earlier this month -- just 24 basis points above the federal funds rate. Players said the two-year note should be 75 basis points above funds when the Fed is neutral.

"The market in general digested what (Greenspan) had to say and now we're back to a range more suitable to where funds are," said Neil Desarno, head government bond trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "There had been a euphoria and ... (Friday) we took it out."
Traders don't forsee any lasting problems in the market as a result of Greenspan's speech. But they said the market did get a wake-up call and realized that it was not invincible after all.
"The market will be more cautious," DeSarno said. "But no one is talking tighthening (anymore)." He added that equities markets have more to be concerned about that than fixed income markets.

Players observed that the market probably would have rallied Friday if there were no Greenspan comments because of a weaker-than-expected rise in nonfarm payrolls in November. And, some said that instead of the long bond continuing its march toward 6.25 percent, the bond will likely stay above 6.40 percent, probably closer to 6.50 percent or higher.
A less rosy picture was evoked by Joseph Carson, chief fixed income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, who believes the market's initial reaction was correct.

Carson said he believes the market has grown too complacent. While only recently the bond market had fretted over a low unemployment rate, oil prices at $25 a barrel and rising lumber prices, he said the market now appears to be shrugging it off.
"The market is creating its own funeral here," he said. "The longer these conditions (buying on dips) stay in place, the more likely what Greenspan talked about happens."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
